extracted.intended_audience: educated coffee-house readers, theatre-goers, periodical readers, and writers (early-18th-century literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Short, prescriptive literary and news-writing guidance as given in an early-18th-century periodical: evaluation and commentary on plays, acting, poetry, operas, portraiture, and the selection/tone of news items. Includes moral and decorum expectations for public life and performances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting: exactly enter into the nature of the part
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor/actress should 'exactly enter into the nature of the part' and present the character with appropriate grace and naturalness (e.g., Mrs. Bignell 'made a very pretty figure, and exactly entered into the nature of the part').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is given to performers who adopt the manners of their role (grace in rusticity, natural behaviour) and who show variety of humour and vivacity. Examples include Mrs. Bignell's successful portrayal and the high praise of Mrs. Verbruggen and Mrs. Mountford for their range. Anti-pattern: artificial or ill-fitting portrayal that fails to embody the character's nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play's moral/educative function
rubrics_metrics.description: A good play, when properly acted before a well-bred audience, 'must raise very proper incitements to good behaviour' and serves as a quick and prevailing method of giving young people sense and breeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theatrical works should conduce to the reformation of manners and public virtue rather than merely entertain; plays that encourage good behaviour are to be valued. Use performance and audience context to amplify moral instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience decorum and reporting of indecorums
rubrics_metrics.description: Public assemblies (church, theatre, etc.) require decorum; improprieties (giggling at church, arriving drunk to a play, flustered or disrespectful behaviour in boxes) are to be noticed and admonished in periodical reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The periodical author promises to record indecorums, improprieties and negligences to encourage reformation of manners. Example admonition: a flustered nobleman who embarrassed his company will be publicly reproved. Anti-pattern: tolerating public impropriety without comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization must fit social context and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Playwrights should draw characters true to the manners of their age and station; introducing a virtuous character that contradicts the known manners of the Court shows ignorance of the social world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating characters (e.g., 'fine gentleman'), ensure their behaviour and morality are credible within the contemporary social milieu. Anti-pattern: inserting implausible virtue or vice that betrays unfamiliarity with real manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre should engage reason and all faculties (critique of spectacle/operas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage is 'an entertainment of the reason and all our faculties'; entertainments that depend chiefly on sensory spectacle (e.g., operas mostly in Italian) risk degenerating the public understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer theatrical forms that engage intellect as well as senses; be cautious of productions that leave the understanding out (foreign-language operas, spectacle without sense). Critics may publish treatises against such forms if they believe these amusements weaken public resolve (e.g., for war).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting skill: variety of humour and natural vivacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Great actors exhibit a wide range of humour and a lively naturalness; variety and vivacity in performance are marks of excellence (e.g., Mrs. Verbruggen excelled through variety and equal vivacity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate performers for their range (ability in low and high characters), natural ease, and energetic delivery. Anti-pattern: a performer limited to a single mode or overly artificial manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should avoid mechanical formulas; favour genuine invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets who follow 'certain and infallible rules' produce mechanical works (e.g., satirical 'Advice to Vanderbank') rather than genuine invention; a poem that recycles stock praises is hackneyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value originality and true invention over formulaic receipts. The text satirizes authors who produce ready-made 'receipts for a poem' and encourages poets to invent rather than transplant worn expedients. Example anti-pattern: composing a poem by assembling canned lines of praise and conventional topoi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodical/news writer prudence: avoid offending great persons
rubrics_metrics.description: As a writer of news one should 'avoid speaking of things which may offend great persons' while still 'not prostitute the liberal sciences'—balance truth-telling with discretion to avoid injuring patrons or powerful readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tact (the author jokingly claims astrological skill) to steer clear of unnecessarily offensive assertions about the powerful; restrict sharper truths to matters not immediately concerning the commonwealth's good. Anti-pattern: gratuitously attacking powerful persons and causing needless offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content selection: variety of matter and style without unjust offence
rubrics_metrics.description: The periodical will 'take anything that offers' for subject-matter, presenting new persons and things and a variety of matter and style, aiming 'to give entertainment for men of pleasure, without offence to those of business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select diverse topics (news, poems, theatrical notices, portraits of persons) and vary style to suit different readers; avoid content that 'ought justly to displease.' Include notices from public assemblies, theatre reports, and social commentary to appeal broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture/representation should capture characteristic force
rubrics_metrics.description: A painter's portrait should represent the sitter's characteristic manner and force (e.g., Jervas's portraits of Clarissa and Chloe represent different kinds of beauty—soft harmony vs piercing irresistible quality—and evoke corresponding effects on admirers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess portraits by how well they convey the specific temperament and social effect of the sitter (pose, dress, expression). Example guidance: choose attributes (shepherdess vs country girl dress, straw hat and riband) that embody the sitter's social and emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire as a means of moral instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire (e.g., the character of Horner in The Country Wife) should expose vice and its progress to instruct readers: by showing the gradual steps to ruin in natural innocence, satire becomes 'a very pleasant and instructive' means of social correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use witty satire to illustrate moral lessons—present vice so that contempt of it is the only defence. Anti-pattern: satire that excuses or fails to mark vice's harms.
